title: The Scholar with the Mountain of Scrolls (KN)
summary: A pedantic scholar arrives with five cartloads of parchment scrolls, boasting of his unmatched learning. Birbal asks one simple question about life.
full_text:
A famous philosopher named Acharya Vashishta arrived in Agra accompanied by five heavy bullock carts loaded with hundreds of leather-bound parchment scrolls, commentaries, and philosophical treatises.

Standing before Emperor Akbar, the scholar pointed proudly to his carts: 'Your Majesty! I have studied thirty thousand volumes! I carry the entire accumulated wisdom of ancient Greece, Persia, Arabia, and Hindustan upon these five carts! There is no question of grammar, metaphysics, or astronomy that I cannot answer!'

Akbar was awestruck by the mountain of learning, but Birbal looked at the scholar with gentle, compassionate eyes.

Birbal asked politely: 'Acharya-ji, your library is magnificent. Tell me—have you read all those thirty thousand volumes?'

'Every single word!' the scholar boasted. 'I spent forty years reading day and night!'

Birbal asked a second question: 'And tell me, Acharya-ji: during those forty years of reading in your study, did you ever plant a single tree to give shade to a weary traveler?'

The scholar blinked: 'No... I had no time for gardening.'

'Did you ever sit by the bed of a sick neighbor and bathe his feverish brow?'

'No... I was studying metaphysics.'

'Did you ever reconcile two brothers who were bitter enemies, or teach a poor orphan how to earn his bread?'

'No... those are petty worldly matters.'

Birbal turned to Emperor Akbar with a gentle sigh:

'Sire, behold this scholar. He is like a sturdy donkey laden with five cartloads of precious sandalwood!

'The donkey carries the sweet sandalwood upon its back, but it knows only the heavy, crushing weight of the wood, without ever enjoying its fragrance or divine sweetness!

'Knowledge that is locked away in scrolls, never translated into love, mercy, charity, and service to human beings, is merely heavy dead cargo!

'A simple peasant who cannot read, but who feeds a starving child and comforts a weeping neighbor, possesses more true wisdom in his little finger than five cartloads of dead philosophy!'

The scholar stood frozen. The mirror of truth pierced his forty years of academic pride. Tears filled his eyes as he realized that in accumulating words, he had forgotten how to live.

The scholar bowed low to Birbal, resolved to open a free school for poor children, and thanked him for awakening his soul.
